articles.body: Greater China Hong Kong’s five-year clock Splash November 16, 2026 0 1 4 minutes read From tax reform and green bunkering to ship registration and a new partnership with Shanghai, the government in Hong Kong is pursuing an increasingly ambitious maritime strategy. The challenge is turning policy commitments into lasting commercial activity. The latest instalment from our new Hong Kong magazine, which is being distributed across the city’s maritime week. Hong Kong’s government is attempting something more ambitious than rescuing a declining container port. It wants to turn the territory into what it calls a “global maritime capital”, earning more from the financing, insuring, managing and fuelling of ships even if fewer containers cross its quays. That change in emphasis has gathered pace throughout 2026. February’s budget proposed fresh shipping incentives, June brought tax legislation, September produced Hong Kong’s first five-year development plan and October has already seen proposed regulatory changes for green bunkering and a new agreement with Shanghai. The latest move came on October 20, when transport and logistics secretary Mable Chan signed a “brother port” cooperation agreement with Shanghai. The two cities intend to coordinate liner services, intermodal logistics, green shipping and maritime professional services. The agreement is significant for a port that has struggled against mainland competition: Hong Kong’s strategy increasingly relies on partnership rather than attempting to regain its former position in the container rankings. The clearest statement of intent came in the 2026-2030 plan and chief executive John Lee’s September policy address. The administration has explicitly called for a transition from “volume to value”, setting targets to reduce emissions from Kwai Tsing’s container terminals by 30% from 2021 levels, establish five green energy corridors and have 7% of Hong Kong-registered ships take up green maritime fuels by 2030. Green bunkering offers the most visible evidence of policy being translated into operations. Hong Kong completed its first methanol bunkering operation in March, followed days later by methanol bunkering alongside container handling at Kwai Tsing. From June 16, vessels carrying, using or bunkering eligible alternative fuels became entitled to port dues reductions of 25% or 50%, while qualifying Hong Kong-registered green-fuel ships can claim HK$60,000 annually for three years. The budget earmarks HK$34m for the incentives. In October the government gazetted measures to expand sea room available for green-fuel bunkering from 645 hectares to 2,877 hectares, including seven new anchorages. This is the sort of unglamorous infrastructure reform that matters to owners and suppliers assessing whether vessels can bunker safely without upsetting schedules. Yet storage and supply remain unfinished business. The administration wants green-fuel storage facilities at Tsing Yi South, with planning procedures scheduled for 2027 and tenders in early 2028. It also intends to announce its first green energy corridor with a mainland city later this year, connecting Chinese fuel production with international shipping demand. A green-fuel trading platform and carbon-accounting framework are also being explored. “Owners will ultimately bunker where fuel is available safely, consistently and at a competitive delivered price,” says Vikrant Gusain, chief executive of Dockendale Group. It is a reminder that incentives cannot substitute for dependable physical supply. Finance + Shipping agenda A second strand involves attracting commercial activity ashore. A bill gazetted in June seeks to improve shipping-related tax concessions, including adjustments to accommodate international minimum-tax rules, and introduce half-rate profits tax for qualifying physical commodity traders. The legislation remains before lawmakers in October. The rationale is that commodity trading produces demand for chartering, insurance, finance and maritime legal services. Simply offering lower tax rates to shipowners will not, by itself, rebuild that ecosystem. Richard Hext, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association, welcomes the administration’s proposed ‘Finance + Shipping’ agenda, which seeks to join ship finance, marine insurance and arbitration into a more compelling package. The government wants more underwriting capacity for specialist marine risks and is supporting the Hong Kong Shipowners Mutual Assurance Association’s development of international business, alongside promotion of the city’s arbitration services. But Hext offers a useful measure of success. “The next phase should be judged by substantive functions, regional headquarters, underwriting authority, credit decisions, trading desks and skilled jobs, and not by company registrations alone,” he says. Ship registration is another target. The government is preparing legislation to permit dual registration arrangements for bareboat-chartered ships, allowing owners to suspend one registration temporarily while a vessel operates under another flag. The objective is to make Hong Kong’s registry more useful to the increasingly complicated leasing and chartering structures of international fleets. The changes remain proposals rather than enacted reforms. At the port At the waterfront, the Port Community System launched in January to connect cargo information across sea, land and air. By September, more than 8,000 enterprises had registered and verified cargo data had supported more than 20 successful trade-finance applications. The next stage promises offshore cargo tracking using blockchain technology, while Kwai Tsing is earmarked for greater use of remotely operated cranes, autonomous electric vehicles and shore power. The city is also seeking new inland cargo through expanded rail-sea and river-sea links and deeper cooperation with Greater Bay Area ports. More direct liner connections to Central and South America are among the government’s priorities. Talent Then there is talent. Lee has proposed a maritime academy built around cooperation between educational institutions and employers, and the five-year plan calls for closer engagement with mainland training institutions and maritime technology researchers. “If I could choose one thing, it would be accelerating our maritime talent strategy,” says Angad Banga, chief executive of The Caravel Group. “Talent takes far longer to develop.” Promotion is part of the offensive too. The tenth Hong Kong Maritime Week takes place in November, with the government, shipowners and the International Chamber of Shipping bringing international executives together in the territory. The strategy is wide-ranging, but the industry still sees gaps in execution and governance. Horace Lo, group managing director of Modern Terminals, identifies “the establishment of a Maritime and Port Authority, and closer collaboration among ports in the GBA” as priorities. Others want faster progress on physical fuel storage and greater evidence that financing and insurance decisions are actually being made locally. Hong Kong now has a more detailed maritime programme than it has had for years. Its credibility will depend not on how many initiatives are announced, but on whether they bring cargo, capital, specialist jobs and commercial authority back to the city. articles.body: Services Top Right Medkon adds Algiers to Turkey–North Africa service November 15, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Medkon KRM / Source: MarineTraffic Medkon Lines has expanded its Turkey–North Africa (TNA) service with the addition of a port call at Algiers, extending the service’s coverage to Algeria alongside its existing connection with Tunisia. According to DynaLiners, the revised service will be operated by a single container vessel with a capacity of approximately 700 TEU, offering sailings every 20 days between Turkey and North Africa. The updated port rotation will be: Istanbul (Ambarli) – Izmit (Yilport) – Aliaga – Algiers – Rades – Istanbul (Ambarli). The addition of Algiers provides another direct connection between Turkish ports and Algeria, while maintaining the service’s existing call at Rades in Tunisia. Medkon already serves the Algerian market through its Turkey–Alger (TAE) service. The latest adjustment therefore expands the company’s coverage of Algeria through the TNA rotation rather than marking its entry into the market. The revised arrangement retains the three Turkish calls at Ambarli, Yilport and Aliaga, with the service now covering two North African destinations. articles.title: US extends Jones Act waiver into February
articles.summary: Washington has extended its Jones Act waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged vessels to continue competing for selected domestic cargo movements between US ports into February next year. The Department of Homeland Security approved the third extension of the waiver introduced in March, according to a...
articles.body: Americas Containers Dry Cargo Operations Regulatory Tankers US extends Jones Act waiver into February Adis Ajdin November 16, 2026 0 61 1 minute read White House White House Washington has extended its Jones Act waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged vessels to continue competing for selected domestic cargo movements between US ports into February next year. The Department of Homeland Security approved the third extension of the waiver introduced in March, according to a November 13 notice from US Customs and Border Protection. The new period starts on November 16. Eligible cargo must be loaded before 11.59 pm Eastern Time on February 14, 2027. Foreign-flagged ships will still need individual approval before undertaking coastwise voyages. Cargo interests must submit vessel availability requests to the relevant US authorities, after which the Maritime Administration will survey the market to determine whether suitable Jones Act-qualified tonnage is available. The requirement keeps the tighter approval system introduced in August rather than restoring the broader exemptions available earlier in the year. The waiver was initially introduced in March amid disruption to US fuel supplies and shipping markets following the outbreak of war with Iran. It allows specified commodities to move between domestic ports aboard vessels that would ordinarily be barred from the trade under the Jones Act. The latest extension has drawn renewed criticism from the American Maritime Partnership, which represents US maritime interests and wants the exemption brought to an end. The group urged Washington to continue scrutinising individual applications, warning against allowing foreign vessels to displace American ships and crews on routine commercial movements. The Jones Act generally reserves domestic waterborne cargo movements for US-built, US-owned and US-flagged vessels meeting the law’s requirements. The extension leaves those restrictions in place outside the approved waiver arrangements. articles.body: Europe Gas Naftomar returns to South Korea for LPG quartet Adis Ajdin November 16, 2026 0 54 1 minute read Naftomar Naftomar Greek gas carrier specialist Naftomar has been linked to an order for four 9,000 cu m semi-refrigerated LPG carriers at HD Hyundai’s medium-sized shipbuilding operation in South Korea .Shipbroking sources have identified the Athens-based owner behind the quartet, with deliveries scheduled between December 2028 and September 2029. No contract price has been reported, and the order has yet to be publicly confirmed by the owner or shipbuilder. The newbuildings would add to Naftomar’s established presence in the smaller gas carrier segment, where it operates a fleet of semi-refrigerated and pressurised vessels alongside larger LPG tonnage. Its existing fleet includes the 2010-built, 9,103 cu m Gaz Explorer and the 2011-built, 9,102 cu m sisters Gaz Concord and Gaz Venture , all built in South Korea. Naftomar has a long history of investing in Korean gas carrier tonnage, including its move into the very large gas carrier segment. In late 2023, the group booked four 93,000 cu m LPG/ammonia carriers at Hanwha Ocean in a deal valued at around $500m, marking one of its largest investments in gas shipping. The latest reported order would add 36,000 cu m of capacity to its smaller gas carrier fleet, with the new vessels arriving over a 10-month period. articles.title: India eases flag rules in push for more tonnage
articles.summary: India has relaxed its ship registration rules, allowing vessels with majority Indian ownership to qualify for the national flag in a move that opens the door to foreign minority investment. The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways has set the ownership threshold at more than 50%, replacing the full qualifying...
articles.body: Asia Operations Regulatory India eases flag rules in push for more tonnage Adis Ajdin November 16, 2026 0 133 1 minute read India has relaxed its ship registration rules, allowing vessels with majority Indian ownership to qualify for the national flag in a move that opens the door to foreign minority investment. The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways has set the ownership threshold at more than 50%, replacing the full qualifying Indian ownership requirement imposed under the previous Merchant Shipping Act. A government notification published in the Gazette of India sets out the new conditions under the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. The threshold applies to legal ownership of shares in the vessel itself, rather than simply the shareholding of a company operating it. Eligible Indian interests can meet the requirement individually or collectively. Qualifying owners include Indian citizens, non-resident Indians, overseas citizens of India, Indian-incorporated companies, cooperatives and limited liability partnerships. Where a non-resident Indian or overseas citizen of India holds the majority interest, an authorised representative based or incorporated in India must be appointed. The change does not automatically give qualifying ships the right to fly the Indian flag. Owners should still complete the registration process and obtain approval from the authorities. The move comes during a wider push by New Delhi to increase Indian-flagged tonnage and strengthen its domestic shipping industry. Splash reported last year that MSC, Maersk and CMA CGM were looking to shift vessels onto the Indian register, while Hapag-Lloyd signed agreements with the government in March covering possible reflagging of up to four ships. India is also building out its state-backed Bharat Container Shipping Line and has launched initiatives targeting ship finance, insurance and domestic shipbuilding. articles.body: Iran claims fresh strike on U.S. base as Hormuz shipping crisis deepens in International Shipping News 15/11/2026 Iran claimed a fresh drone strike against a U.S. military facility in Bahrain on Sunday, as mine incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia heightened regional tensions. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said six drones targeted an air-defense radar at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base. Bahrain issued repeated security alerts, but U.S. Central Command had not confirmed the latest claim. The U.S. military denied an earlier Iranian claim of damage at the facility, saying it intercepted two drones without casualties or damage. The escalation followed reports from Iran’s navy that two more tankers struck mines and caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz, bringing the reported total to seven incidents within 24 hours. Tehran says ships using routes without Iranian authorization are violating its restrictions. Iranian officials have linked reopening the waterway to an end to the U.S. naval blockade and acceptance of seven conditions for an agreement. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Tehran remained prepared for negotiations or renewed conflict, warning that its armed forces would determine the scope of any response to further U.S. action. The disruption extends beyond energy shipments. A senior United Nations official urged Washington and Tehran to permit fertilizer cargoes through Hormuz, warning that missed planting seasons could leave 45 million people facing severe food insecurity. Fertilizer prices have risen 30% since the blockades, the official said. In Saudi Arabia, a Saudi-led coalition reported intercepting two ballistic missiles heading toward Riyadh and three Houthi drones over the kingdom’s eastern region. The Houthis separately claimed to have downed a Saudi reconnaissance aircraft over Yemen’s al-Jawf province. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards also claimed to have destroyed a U.S. MQ-1 drone over Qeshm Island, an assertion not independently verified. Diplomatic attention now turns to the November 18-19 APEC summit in Shenzhen, where U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to discuss the Iran war with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump recently reassigned Vice President JD Vance from Iran negotiations and said reaching a deal was no longer a priority. Source: Investing.com 2026-11-15 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: ITEF Launches Collective Bargaining Framework and Calls for Stronger Seafarers’ Welfare and Maritime Safety Standards
articles.summary: The International Transport Employees Federation (ITEF) has launched a comprehensive Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) Framework for seafarers, incorporating relevant provisions of the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 (MLC 2006), and proposing the International Labour Organization (ILO)-recommended minimum wage...
articles.body: ITEF Launches Collective Bargaining Framework and Calls for Stronger Seafarers’ Welfare and Maritime Safety Standards in International Shipping News 15/11/2026 The International Transport Employees Federation (ITEF) has launched a comprehensive Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) Framework for seafarers, incorporating relevant provisions of the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 (MLC 2006), and proposing the International Labour Organization (ILO)-recommended minimum wage scale as a benchmark for seafarers’ remuneration. The initiative marks a significant step towards strengthening collective representation, promoting fair employment conditions and advancing internationally recognised labour and welfare standards across the maritime industry. The launch forms part of ITEF’s broader mission to establish a stronger, coordinated national platform for seafarers’ trade unions, maritime welfare organisations and transport workers’ representatives in India. The Federation seeks to address longstanding challenges confronting seafarers, including wage disputes, employment exploitation, onboard harassment, inadequate working and living conditions, unsafe vessels and gaps in welfare protection. As part of its efforts to address critical issues affecting the maritime workforce, an ITEF delegation met senior officials of the Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA), Government of India, including Shri Shyam Jagannathan, IAS, Director General of Maritime Administration; Shri Killi Mohana Rao, Chief Surveyor-cum-Additional Director General; and Capt. S. I. Abul Kalam Azad, Nautical Adviser-cum-Additional Director General. The delegation submitted representations and held detailed discussions on the welfare and safety of Indian seafarers serving onboard vessels in Indian waters and across international shipping routes. Key concerns included onboard harassment, unpaid wages, unsafe working conditions, substandard vessels, MLC 2006 violations and the need for stronger regulatory enforcement. The delegation also brought to the attention of the Nautical Adviser and PSC Chief Surveyor, DGMA, Government of India that seafarers unions and welfare organisations are receiving numerous complaints from seafarers and their dependants concerning employment-related exploitation, delayed payment of wages, poor onboard conditions and other welfare violations. Serious concern was expressed over substandard vessels continuing to visit Indian ports and enter Indian waters, potentially endangering the lives of seafarers and the safety of maritime operations. In view of these concerns, the delegation strongly urged the DGMA authorities to increase and strengthen Port State Control (PSC) inspections at all Indian ports, including unannounced inspections. It emphasised that inspections should not be limited to the technical condition of vessels but should also give due importance to crew welfare, working and living conditions, safety equipment, seaworthiness and compliance with MLC 2006. The delegation called for appropriate action against established violations. ITEF Pledges Collective Bargaining with Shipping Companies Shri Amar Singh Thakur, General Secretary of the All India Seafarers and General Workers Union, and Shri Jagan Mohan Naidu, General Secretary of the Republican Maritime Union, stated that ITEF is committed to strengthening the collective bargaining rights of seafarers and advancing employment conditions in line with recognised international maritime labour standards. They said the Federation intends to engage directly with shipowners, ship managers and shipping companies to facilitate negotiations and the conclusion of Collective Bargaining Agreements through its affiliated and member seafarers’ trade unions. Stronger Port State Control Inspections Urged Across India’s Major and Minor Ports During the meeting with the maritime administration the delegation urged Shri Killi Mohana Rao, Chief Surveyor-cum-Additional Director General, and Capt. S. I. Abul Kalam Azad, Nautical Adviser-cum-Additional Director General (Nautical), to strengthen Port State Control (PSC) inspections across all major and minor ports in India. They emphasised the need for more effective vessel inspections to ensure that shipping companies maintain appropriate standards of vessel seaworthiness, operational safety and compliance with international maritime regulations. They further stressed that inspections should give due importance to seafarers’ working and living conditions, onboard safety arrangements and compliance with the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 (MLC 2006). ITEF called for stronger regulatory oversight and appropriate enforcement action against vessels found to have deficiencies or violations, emphasising that vessel safety and seafarers’ welfare must be treated as complementary priorities in maritime operations. Through collective action, institutional cooperation and international engagement, ITEF aims to strengthen the voice of seafarers and contribute to a safer, fairer and more accountable global maritime industry. articles.body: Acta Marine Takes Delivery of Acta Aquarius, Completing Four-Vessel Newbuild Programme in International Shipping News 15/11/2026 Acta Marine proudly announces the delivery of Acta Aquarius, the fourth and final vessel in its series of next-generation Walk-to-Work (W2W) DP2 Construction Service Operation Vessels (CSOVs), built by Tersan Shipyard in Yalova, Turkey. Following the deliveries of Acta Pegasus, Acta Hercules and Acta Gemini, Acta Aquarius completes an important fleet expansion programme and represents another step in Acta Marine’s continued investment in a modern and sustainable fleet. As the final vessel in the series, Acta Aquarius marks an important milestone in Acta Marine’s ambition to support the offshore energy sector with increasingly sustainable vessel solutions. Acta Aquarius is certified and operates as dual-fuel methanol powered vessel. Combined with her battery power system, this supports Acta Marine’s pathway towards lower-emission offshore operations, while maintaining the safety, reliability and efficiency at the core of its Walk-to-Work services. Acta Aquarius is accompanied by daughter craft Acta Situla, which was delivered to Acta Marine earlier this year in June. Rob Boer, CEO of Acta Marine, commented: “The delivery of Acta Aquarius is a proud moment for Acta Marine and marks the completion of our four-vessel newbuild programme with Tersan Shipyard. Together, these vessels represent an important investment in the future of our fleet and strengthen our ability to support our clients in the offshore wind industry. With dual-fuel methanol propulsion capability, Acta Aquarius marks an important step towards more sustainable offshore operations, significantly reducing CO2 emissions, while continuing to provide the safe, reliable and efficient services our clients expect from us.” With the four-vessel newbuild programme now complete, Acta Marine looks forward to deploying Acta Aquarius and continuing to support the growth of offshore wind with safe, reliable and increasingly sustainable offshore solutions. articles.body: HJ Shipbuilding & Construction posts 65.9 billion won Q3 operating profit in Shipbuilding News 15/11/2026 Operating profit for HJ Shipbuilding & Construction(097230) in the third quarter of this year (July–September) came to 65.9 billion won. Improved profitability in the shipbuilding institutional sector drove the result. Compared with the same period last year, revenue increased 46.3%, operating profit 837.1%, and net profit 4,432.7%. In the shipbuilding institutional sector, revenue for January–September was 1.1297 trillion won and operating profit was 149.7 billion won. Revenue grew as construction of eco-friendly, high value-added container ships ramped up. Specialty ship projects, including the U.S. Navy MRO (maintenance, repair and overhaul) business, also generated steady profit. In the construction institutional sector, revenue for January–September was 874.2 billion won and operating profit was 5.6 billion won. The company remained in the black by maintaining a stable business base focused on public works, civil engineering, and housing. articles.title: US midterms won’t derail Venezuela’s oil recovery but could delay greenfield upside
articles.summary: The Democratic victory in the 2026 US midterm elections has given the party control of both chambers of Congress, limiting President Trump’s domestic agenda from January 2027. However, foreign policy remains largely within the president’s remit, as demonstrated by his interventions in Venezuela this year, from the...
articles.body: US midterms won’t derail Venezuela’s oil recovery but could delay greenfield upside in Oil & Companies News 15/11/2026 The Democratic victory in the 2026 US midterm elections has given the party control of both chambers of Congress, limiting President Trump’s domestic agenda from January 2027. However, foreign policy remains largely within the president’s remit, as demonstrated by his interventions in Venezuela this year, from the capture of Nicolas Maduro to the reopening of the country’s oil sector. These developments have highlighted how closely Venezuela’s oil recovery is tied to decisions in Washington. However, Rystad Energy’s analysis suggests that Venezuela’s near-term oil recovery is unlikely to be derailed by the latest election result. The bigger risk lies further down the line, as increased congressional scrutiny could delay around 0.5 million bpd of potential production growth until after 2040. Venezuela’s near-term recovery is being driven primarily by brownfield activity, including well reactivations, workovers and infill drilling. These projects have shorter lead times and require fewer new approvals, supporting crude production growth from approximately 1.2 million bpd in October 2026 to around 1.5 million bpd by 2028, an increase of roughly 300,000 bpd. Sanctions implementation and licensing by the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) also remain largely under executive control, limiting what a Democratic Congress can change directly. The picture becomes less certain further out, as growth increasingly depends on greenfield developments, larger investment commitments and the operators selected to deliver them. Rystad Energy’s existing upside scenario sees Venezuelan production approaching 3 million bpd by 2040 assuming stronger prices and continued policy support. A new sensitivity following the midterm result suggests greater congressional scrutiny could delay selected greenfield projects by one to three years, pushing around 0.5 million bpd of potential 2040 production further out. The impact is concentrated in longer-cycle projects rather than the brownfield-led recovery expected over the next few years. However, that growth will be harder to deliver if political scrutiny delays or challenges operators’ ability to develop their assets. North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) is a case in point. Its three production participation contracts have lifted combined output from roughly 90,000 barrels per day (bpd) at the end of 2024 to nearly 200,000 bpd currently, led by Petrozamora. The company is already facing questions from Democratic lawmakers over its selection and the legal basis for its agreements, raising broader questions about Venezuela’s operating environment and its ability to attract investment to sustain longer-term recovery. Greater scrutiny doesn’t change Venezuela’s underlying resource potential. Most of the near-term recovery involves bringing existing wells back online, which doesn’t require congressional approval, so I wouldn’t expect the midterms to slow that down. The bigger risk is to greenfield projects, which could be delayed by several years. The oil isn’t going anywhere, but it may take longer to reach the market. ExxonMobil’s recently announced MOU with PDVSA remains at an early stage, with no committed capital or development timetable yet disclosed; this suggests interest in unlocking Venezuela’s petroleum potential rather than any concrete investment commitments. A longer-term complication, however, is Venezuela’s own election. A new government could revisit the contracts signed under the interim administration, creating uncertainty for projects that require 10 to 20 years of political and regulatory stability,” Radhika Bansal, Senior Vice President, Upstream Research, Rystad Energy The political reset in January has also reshaped Venezuela’s oil export patterns, with a much larger share of the country’s crude now heading to the US and India. Together, the two countries accounted for around three-quarters of Venezuelan crude exports over the period shown. India, in particular, presents an opportunity for Venezuela to regain market share from Russia, which has become a major supplier of crude oil to the country since the outbreak of the war in Ukraine. At the same time, US policy continues to place greater pressure on buyers of Russian crude than on those purchasing Venezuelan oil. However, the change isn’t like-for-like as Venezuela’s main export grade, Merey, is a heavy, high-sulfur crude that is significantly thicker and more difficult to process than Russian Urals. It requires specialized refinery equipment to turn it into usable fuels, meaning only India’s more complex refineries can readily absorb additional volumes. Higher shipping costs to Asia also make Venezuelan crude less competitive when Russian Urals is available at steep discounts. Ultimately, Venezuela’s ability to capture a larger share of India’s imports will depend on both commercial economics and US policy. If Washington continues to apply greater pressure on Russian crude buyers while allowing Venezuelan trade to expand, Venezuela could gain a competitive advantage. However, differences in crude quality, refinery compatibility and freight costs mean it is unlikely to replace Russian barrels one-for-one. For the US midterms, the key point is that the election result is unlikely to disrupt Venezuelan exports in the near term, as any change in congressional control would not automatically alter existing trade flows or the current policy framework. From a geopolitical perspective, Venezuela’s next election could become an increasingly important signpost for oil markets. No date has been agreed, although Washington has outlined a transition roadmap involving reforms to the judiciary and electoral authorities, followed by the declaration of a presidential vacancy and new elections. A Democratic victory in the US midterms could increase pressure on Trump to accelerate this process. Democrats have already questioned the lack of a clear democratic roadmap and could use congressional hearings, funding negotiations and oversight powers to demand firmer commitments. While their ability to dictate Venezuela’s electoral calendar remains limited, they could raise the political cost of delaying the transition. President Trump, however, faces a dilemma: holding elections sooner would allow him to claim credit for restoring democracy in Venezuela and bolster his foreign policy legacy, but could also put existing oil agreements at risk. A newly elected government could revisit deals reached with interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez, creating uncertainty for investors and potentially delaying planned projects. Allowing more time for economic recovery and investment before holding elections may therefore suit the Trump administration, particularly if it gives existing commercial arrangements time to take hold before a new government comes to power. Source: Rystad Energy 2026-11-15 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: However, foreign policy remains largely within the president’s remit, as demonstrated by his interventions in Venezuela this year, from the capture of Nicolas Maduro to the reopening of the country’s oil sector.
These developments have highlighted how closely Venezuela’s oil recovery is tied to decisions in Washington.
However, Rystad Energy’s analysis suggests that Venezuela’s near-term oil recovery is unlikely to be derailed by the latest election result.

articles.title: THINK Ahead: How to survive without AI
articles.summary: Seriously, what are we supposed to do when an AI chatbot breaks down? Who’s going to tell me I’ve made a “really insightful point” after a seven-word prompt, with three words spelled incorrectly? Who’s going to suggest a clickbait headline, like “Unpacking a world without Copilot: James Smith’s THINK Ahead at a...
articles.body: THINK Ahead: How to survive without AI in Stock News 15/11/2026 Seriously, what are we supposed to do when an AI chatbot breaks down? Who’s going to tell me I’ve made a “really insightful point” after a seven-word prompt, with three words spelled incorrectly? Who’s going to suggest a clickbait headline, like “Unpacking a world without Copilot: James Smith’s THINK Ahead at a crossroads”? And, most importantly, who’s going to ask whether I’d like the answer turned into a table? After briefly confronting the terrifying prospect of thinking for ourselves, I thought I’d have a go at doing AI’s job. So, after today’s outage, here’s a timely prompt: Can the global economy survive without AI in 2027? Connecting the dots… Piecing it all together… Pretending to think deeply… That’s a fascinating question! (Predictable.) Let’s break it down into four key areas. Because everything has to be broken down into four key areas… The resilience question If today’s Microsoft outage tells us anything, it’s that we probably underestimate the economic risks of critical infrastructure failing. At our Global Outlook webinar this week, just 2% of the audience picked new supply shocks, including cyberattacks, as the biggest risk for 2027. A rather larger 34% chose an AI bubble bursting and stock markets crashing. More on that shortly. Now, one chatbot crashing out for a few hours isn’t going to move global GDP. Spain’s huge blackout in 2025 barely registered in the growth figures. But as we argued in our outlook, the damage from electricity, payments or communications outages could rise disproportionately if they become more frequent or widespread. It starts to hit confidence. And businesses are forced to spend more insulating themselves. One data centre owner told me this week that they keep 48 hours’ worth of diesel on site in case the power conks out. That sort of contingency doesn’t come cheap. But the flipside is that businesses are building up resilience against supply shocks like the Iran war – or a ‘moat’, as our AI overlords like to say. Greater preparedness, including more hedging, is one leading explanation for why European core inflation has remained remarkably subdued so far. ‘Unpacking’ (sorry) the growth impact Everyone talks about the boost AI investment has given the US economy. And my colleague James Knightley wrote in our outlook this week that this is likely to continue into 2027. What gets talked about less is the impact it’s having on Europe. Partly, that’s because the story is mixed. As a nice chart from my colleague Pablo Muylle showed this week, not everyone is enjoying a Netherlands/ASML-style boost to manufacturing. It’s a similar story for data centres, which are contributing around 0.1-0.2pp to year-on-year eurozone growth if you take the IT sector as a proxy. By contrast, as we saw in this week’s GDP data, the data centre rollout in the UK is adding around 0.4pps to the roughly 2% annual growth we’re seeing. That should remain a tailwind next year and there’s clearly scope for a positive surprise. The more intriguing question is what’s happening outside the server farms. UK output across parts of professional services, from law to accountancy, has shot up remarkably quickly this year and in apparent unison. Is that AI productivity coming through? I suspect that is some, though not all, of what’s going on. Or as AI would put it, “The answer is nuanced.” Thanks for that… What if the AI bubble bursts? Never ask an AI chatbot if AI is a bubble. It hurts our feelings. But… if we did get a proper bear market in US equities, the problems are likely to extend well beyond tech. We wrote about this in our Outlook report this week. Remember what happened after the dotcom bust, when non-tech investment fell harder than tech itself, on account of wider credit spreads and tighter lending standards. And were it to happen – not our base case – then it would have big ramifications for the Fed, which has built a rate hike rationale linked heavily to the solid equity market. My FX colleagues reckon the impact on the dollar would depend not only on that interest rate story, but whether an equity correction threatens financial stability. If it does, the dollar could still attract some safe haven flows, though in general they reckon JPY and CHF are the more obvious beneficiaries of a serious sell-off. Read more in their FX Outlook hot off the press this week – and sign up for the team’s webinar on Monday. And what about inflation? Fed Governor Chris Waller suggested this week that AI is putting upward pressure on inflation. It helped form the basis of his suggestion that rates could rise by 50bp in December, and contributed to the 32bp rise in short-dated US rates this week. But is it true? There are admittedly many ways AI could be influencing inflation, but the evidence of “chipflation” is pretty flimsy so far. Even using a generous definition of electronics and IT hardware, those categories are still dragging US inflation down, not up. So are cars, despite being stuffed with semiconductors. The inflation figures are undoubtedly problematic; a 0.4pp rise in the Fed’s preferred metric of core inflation can’t be ruled out for October. But AI really isn’t the main event here. So there you have it. Now, would you like me to summarise that in five bullet points, adopt a more professional tone, or turn it into a PowerPoint presentation featuring an alarming amount of purple? James Smith THINK Ahead in developed markets United States (James Knightley) Financial markets have aggressively repriced the outlook for Federal Reserve policy in the wake of hawkish comments from officials and a hotter-than-anticipated core CPI print. There are several Fed officials scheduled to speak over the coming week, despite Chair Kevin Warsh’s desire for less forward guidance, and they will retain a hawkish bias. We fully expect a 25bp rate hike at the December FOMC meeting, but the Fed will have a pre-release copy of the November inflation report, and that should look very benign given steep declines in gasoline prices. Hence, we don’t see much likelihood of a mooted 50bp hike. Retail Sales/Industrial Output (Tue): In terms of data, we will have October retail sales, which will be held down by weak auto sales. Gasoline sales are likely to be close to flat. In real terms, we could see total sales fall. Manufacturing output should continue growing, boosted by a strong performance from advanced manufacturing tied to the tech/AI rollout. Some traditional, heavy energy usage sectors, such as steel and glass, should also perform well given their comparative advantage over European and Asian producers, who are having to deal with sharply higher energy costs. United Kingdom (James Smith) Inflation (Wed): We expect headline inflation to nudge higher on a small rise in the quarterly energy price cap and a further 4% rise in fuel costs. It won’t be until January that we see the full impact of higher natural gas prices when household energy bills are set to rise by circa 25%, something that’s likely to be formally confirmed in the coming days. That’s likely to take headline CPI to just shy of 4.5% early next year. However, for now, second-round effects look minimal. We don’t expect further signs of that in October’s data; food inflation is likely to stay unchanged in year-on-year terms. UK-EU summit (Fri): A deal is widely expected on 20 November to bring the UK closer to Europe, via agreements to reduce checks/paperwork on agricultural goods, align on emissions trading, and increase youth mobility. We’ll be looking for any clues about PM Burnham’s willingness to go further, and what these deals tell us about his willingness to compromise on key issues of migration and regulatory alignment. That will hint at how close he might be prepared to go to the single market in future. Source: ING 2026-11-15 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.summary: Prolonged U.S. Congressional scrutiny of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy raises the stakes for already tense relations between the world’s two largest economies. Nvidia’s Huang resigned Thursday, and agreed to testify before Congress sometime before Thanksgiving on Nov. 26. House...
articles.body: How the Jensen Huang affair changes the outlook for U.S.-China relations in World Economy News 15/11/2026 Prolonged U.S. Congressional scrutiny of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy raises the stakes for already tense relations between the world’s two largest economies. Nvidia’s Huang resigned Thursday, and agreed to testify before Congress sometime before Thanksgiving on Nov. 26. House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., told reporters there could be “public hearings for other people or other things down road.” “I worry this incident will deteriorate the atmosphere dramatically in Washington against China, and also export control matters, and also the Trump administration in its way of dealing with China,” said a Beijing-based foreign policy researcher, who requested anonymity as academics risk discipline or even removal for speaking to the media. The researcher warned of a possible return to a situation like that in the 1990s, when a “Chinese-American” nuclear physicist was suspected of sharing nuclear secrets with the Chinese government, resulting in a federal prosecution. The court ultimately dismissed all but one of 59 counts. Now the bilateral relationship, supported by a fragile trade truce, faces another espionage allegation. And this time it’s around the tech executive at the heart of the U.S.-China competition over artificial intelligence. “This isn’t really about Jensen,” said Mitch Presnick, non-resident honorary fellow on the Chinese economy, Center for China Analysis at the Asia Society. He noted how some in Washington prefer measures to exclude China and disagreed with the semiconductor executive’s message that American technology needed to be used in China in order to remain relevant to global tech development. Washington started to restrict Nvidia’s ability to sell advanced chips to China in 2022. But the Trump administration eased many Biden-era restrictions in 2025. Meanwhile, Nvidia’s Huang advocated his views across a spectrum of markets from the U.S. to China to Taiwan to Germany. At the peak of his influence, he shared a banquet table in September with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a summit in Washington, D.C. The two presidents are next expected to meet alongside the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting from Nov. 18 to 19 in Shenzhen, China. The political landscape has swiftly changed, with Democrats sweeping U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3 and turmoil over subsequent reports about Huang’s alleged Beijing spy connection. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair over the weekend. It remains unclear whether any sensitive information was shared. China’s Foreign Ministry has called the “Chinese spy” allegation unfounded “smears against China.” “The U.S. should stop fabricating the “Chinese spy” narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions,” spokeswoman Mao Ning said Thursday, according to an official English translation. More controls, more unease But the immediate outcome, analysts predict, is more of the U.S. restrictions that China doesn’t want. “The Nvidia scandal has destroyed the credibility of the biggest corporate lobbyist against U.S. export controls on China,” said Arthur Kroeber, partner, Gavekal Dragonomics. “There is now a good chance that Congress will tighten up those rules before the end of this year.” Looking ahead, Kroeber warned Beijing could cut off supplies of rare earths or chipmaking materials if the U.S. tried to restrict China further with the MATCH Act or Affiliates Rule. The measures could, respectively, limit Beijing’s access to key tech suppliers in the Netherlands and Japan, and drastically expand export controls to include many subsidiaries. “So when Trump and Xi meet next week in Shenzhen they will probably agree to keep the uneasy U.S.-China truce going,” Kroeber said. “It will just keep getting more and more uneasy.” ‘Spy balloon’ redux Pressuring China has been a rare area of bipartisan agreement in Washington. Beijing has meanwhile ramped up homegrown alternatives to U.S. tech since Washington restricted Nvidia’s ability to sell advanced chips to China in 2022. And even Trump’s approval of some Nvidia sales had yet to translate into meaningful orders from China. “We are going to see the two countries start to decouple again in terms of technology,” George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice, The Asia Group, said Thursday, noting “China will double-down on self-reliance.” “I begin to feel the Jensen Huang case feels like more like another ‘spy balloon’ case,” he said. In early 2023, during the Biden administration, the U.S. shot down what it described as a Chinese surveillance balloon. Beijing called it a weather balloon that had blown off course. But the incident delayed then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken’s trip to China by more than four months, following limited engagement amid Covid-19 travel restrictions. Fast-forward to the Huang affair, and “the timing is no accident here,” Presnick said. “We’re talking about a very curious set of coincidences, and also the fact that the information came through unnamed sources, and there were other things that were strange about it.” Days after the U.S. midterms, The Financial Times and The New York Times reported, citing sources, that U.S. government intelligence believe China’s Ministry of State Security recruited businesswoman Alice Huang to gather information on then-CEO of Nvidia Jensen Huang. “Obviously somebody was looking to do this, and they wanted to … make the discussion about espionage, and not about American competitiveness,” Presnick said. “The U.S. is thinking [in terms of] U.S. and China, but that’s not what China is thinking,” he said, pointing to Beijing’s trade with fast-growing non-Western economies in Africa and Southeast Asia. articles.title: Rates on the brink: 3 calls for 2027
articles.summary: ING’s base call: Renewed upward pressure on long rates, but it ultimately wanes We expect upward pressure on Treasury yields to persist into early 2027, with AI-driven productivity growth, large fiscal deficits and sticky inflation potentially pushing the 10-year towards 5.25-5.50%. The turn should come later as...
articles.body: Rates on the brink: 3 calls for 2027 in World Economy News 15/11/2026 ING’s base call: Renewed upward pressure on long rates, but it ultimately wanes We expect upward pressure on Treasury yields to persist into early 2027, with AI-driven productivity growth, large fiscal deficits and sticky inflation potentially pushing the 10-year towards 5.25-5.50%. The turn should come later as inflation softens and Fed easing expectations return, pulling yields towards 4.50-4.75%. Inflation remains the key threat heading into 2027. For euro rates, second-round inflation concerns could push 10yr swaps above 4%, but we think markets have gone too far in pricing an ECB terminal rate above 3%. Our end-2027 baseline remains 2.5%, while downside for longer-dated rates looks more limited. AI is an upside risk. France remains the focus in sovereign spreads, with elevated risk premia likely into the elections and some widening elsewhere. But it could also offer the biggest subsequent rally: once the elections pass, receding fears of another eurozone crisis should leave considerable room for French spreads to retrace. Our risky call: Long tenor rates just keep on rising through 2027 There are three credible routes to 6% Treasuries and 4% Bunds. First, inflation. Another energy shock, El Niño disruption or simply more persistent underlying inflation could keep central banks tighter for longer, pushing yields higher across the curve Second, AI. A genuine economy-wide productivity boom could lift potential growth and equilibrium real rates. The dot-com era offers a precedent: strong US growth helped push 10-year Treasury yields above 6% despite relatively benign inflation expectations. A comparable AI-driven productivity shock could have a similar effect. Third, fiscal risk. A sharp deterioration in confidence over US and European fiscal trajectories could generate significant government-bond underperformance versus swaps. In this scenario, the move toward 6% and 4% would reflect rising fiscal and term premia rather than expectations of tighter monetary policy. Our bold call: Long tenor rates are forced to lurch lower on official sector intervention At the extreme, policymakers could decide that rising bond yields pose an unacceptable threat to financial stability. In the eurozone, that could mean the ECB overlooking fiscal recklessness and prioritising the stability of the system and the euro. Existing programmes leave it with considerable firepower to contain yields and fragmentation. The US has its own levers. The Treasury could cut long-end issuance and shift financing towards the front end, while the Fed could keep the funds rate sufficiently low to preserve cheap funding and counter market stress. Taken to its extreme, renewed Fed bond buying could push the desired yield structure into place. The paradox is that policies designed to protect the system could generate even greater systemic risk through de facto yield curve control. For the US, the aim would be a generic funding rate below 4%, ideally around 3.5%. For the eurozone, the result would likely be yield containment, with German yields ultimately trading broadly in line with Treasuries. Source: ING 2026-11-15 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

Romanian Interior Ministry/Handout via REUTERS BUCHAREST, Nov 15 (Reuters) – Drones have struck three commercial ships in the Black Sea near Romania’s Sulina canal , Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said on Sunday, adding that his armed forces had scrambled fighter jets twice. Defence Minister Stefan Radu Oprea said there were no casualties and that the ships’ crews had managed to control the fires on board after the strikes late on Saturday. A growing series of deadly strikes on merchant ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria shows how the escalating maritime war between Russia and Ukraine is expanding into a major challenge for the transatlantic alliance in the Black Sea. The Sulina canal is a key Romanian shipping lane which links the Danube river to the Black Sea and is used by Ukraine for exports. Romanian officials did not identify the origin of the drones but said they were a direct consequence of Russia’s war in Ukraine . “These incidents are unacceptable and constitute a violation of international law,” Niculescu said. “They reflect the deteriorating security situation caused by Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.” Related Article: IMO Warns of Mounting Human Toll as Attacks on Commercial Shipping Continue Russia has denied targeting Ukraine’s neighbours with drones. Oprea said the three struck ships were Greek-flagged oil and chemical tanker Evia Petrol V, bulk carrier Marsol and oil products tanker Ali Najafov, both under the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis. Evia Petrol V and Marsol were struck 4 and 5 nautical miles southeast of the Sulina canal, the defence ministry said, inside Romanian territorial waters. Oprea said a separate general cargo ship was hit by a drone late on Friday, also with no casualties. Private television station Digi24 said the vessel was Palau-flagged general cargo ship Larissa 1. “On Tuesday and Wednesday I will be in Brussels for the meeting with my fellow (defence) ministers,” Oprea said. “We need the solidarity of our allies, shown through patrols with surveillance aircraft and through equipment for counter-drone warfare.” France temporarily relocated the Atlantique 2 maritime patrols aircraft to Romania after it asked for reinforcement. Join the leading maritime news network Photo credit: Tow Boaters Facebook group The captain and crew of the American Heritage , along with tugboat operators and first responders who rushed to the scene, are being hailed as heroes following Friday’s dramatic collision on the Mississippi River that left the river cruise ship capsized but everyone aboard alive. American Cruise Lines singled out Captain Leonard Stewart, who remained on the bridge as the vessel overturned after being struck by the tanker Atlantic Asphalt at the Port of New Orleans on November 13. “The fast actions of Captain Leonard Stewart and our crew allowed for a rapid evacuation of the vessel,” the company said in a statement Saturday. “Captain Stewart remained on the bridge as the vessel capsized, calling for aid and keeping the ship alongside the dock for as long as possible.” The collision occurred at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time, just below the Crescent City Connection bridge. The impact caused the American Heritage to take on water and eventually roll onto its side, sending passengers and crew into the Mississippi River. As the riverboat began to capsize, help arrived from nearly every direction. Harbor tugs, towboats and other working vessels raced toward the scene, joining the U.S. Coast Guard, Port of New Orleans Harbor Police, New Orleans Fire Department and other emergency responders in a massive rescue operation. AIS data and local reports showed crews from Moran Towing, Crescent Towing, Cooper Mooring, John W. Stone Oil Distributor and Canal Barge Co. responding within minutes of the collision. Among the vessels identified near the scene were Moran’s Becky S , Crescent Towing’s Mardi Gras and G. Shelby Friedrichs , the E.N. Bisso tug Marauder , and several Stone Oil towboats, including Presager , Madison Stone , Stephanie Stone and Stone Power . Canal Barge’s Elly Lane was also among the vessels identified, along with the Port of New Orleans fireboat Gen. Roy S. Kelley . While AIS positions alone do not establish the specific actions taken by every vessel, footage and accounts from the scene show working boats joining emergency craft in the rescue effort. Captain Kenny Brown of The Maritime Throwdown praised the private-sector crews whose contributions can sometimes be overlooked amid the attention given to government emergency responders. “When something goes wrong on the river, the first boats you usually see on scene are towboats and tugs,” Brown wrote. “Nobody calls them in. They’re already there, and they turn toward the trouble.” Brown credited the captains, pilots and deckhands who maneuvered their vessels into position and helped with the response. “To the captains who made the call, the pilots who held those boats steady, and the deckhands out on the deck with life rings and pike poles in hand: that’s courage, and the river saw it.” The response was extraordinary in its speed and scale. New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said 87 passengers and crew members were able to disembark before the American Heritage capsized. It then took approximately 30 to 45 minutes for rescuers to pull the remaining people from the river and account for everyone. Mayor Helena Moreno described the outcome as a “miracle on the Mississippi,” crediting the coordinated efforts of government responders and nearby vessels that voluntarily joined the rescue. All passengers and crew were accounted for, with no fatalities. Thirty-two people, including two Harbor Police officers, were transported to hospitals. Eight remained hospitalized as of Saturday, according to local officials. American Cruise Lines thanked the Coast Guard, Port of New Orleans, New Orleans Police Department and other agencies involved in the response. “We are proud of our crew and grateful for the first responders,” the company said, adding that it would continue cooperating with authorities through the investigation and salvage effort. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the collision, including reports that the Atlantic Asphalt may have experienced a steering failure before striking the docked riverboat. The cause has not been determined. The American Heritage remains partially submerged alongside the riverfront, with salvage operations expected to take weeks. For Brown, the incident also underscored the importance of maritime safety training, emergency drills and the ability to respond instinctively when seconds matter. “Practice until it’s muscle memory,” he wrote. “You don’t rise to the occasion. You fall back on your training.” The outcome in New Orleans was a reminder of the professionalism found across the maritime industry, from passenger vessel crews to the working mariners aboard the tugs and towboats that keep the Mississippi River moving. articles.body: CMA CGM has announced new Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) covering shipments from the Far East to South Africa and from Europe and the Mediterranean to Latin America and the Caribbean, with implementation dates in November and December 2026. The French container shipping company will introduce a surcharge of US$650 per TEU on shipments from the Far East to South Africa, effective from 15 November 2026. The measure applies to all cargo types and will remain in place until further notice. The surcharge will be determined by the loading date and covers cargo originating from Far East ports and destined for South Africa. New surcharges from Europe and Mediterranean to the Americas In a separate announcement, CMA CGM confirmed additional Peak Season Surcharges (PSS 02) on shipments from Northern Europe, the Mediterranean, North Africa and the Black Sea to destinations across Latin America and the Caribbean. The new charges will take effect on 7 December 2026, based on the loading date, and will remain applicable until further notice. All three measures apply exclusively to short-term contracts and cover all cargo types. For shipments originating in Northern Europe, excluding Portugal, and destined for the west coast of South America, the carrier will apply a surcharge of €200 per unit. A surcharge of €200 per unit will also apply to shipments originating from Mediterranean ports in Spain, Italy and France, as well as the Adriatic and Portugal. The measure covers destinations on the west coast of South America, the west coasts of Central America and Mexico, the east coast of Central America and the Caribbean, excluding the French West Indies. It also covers the Leeward Islands, excluding Gustavia and Philipsburg, and the Windward Islands. For shipments originating from the Eastern Mediterranean, Adriatic, North Africa and Black Sea, CMA CGM has announced a surcharge of US$200 per unit. This measure applies to the same destination regions, including the west coast of South America, the west coasts of Central America and Mexico, the east coast of Central America and the Caribbean, subject to the stated exclusions for the French West Indies, Gustavia and Philipsburg. The December surcharges will apply in addition to the carrier’s existing freight charges under the relevant contract terms. CMA CGM has not specified an expiry date for either announcement, with both measures remaining in effect until further notice.

articles.title: Sea-Intelligence: Is 2026 TP Peak Season Driven by AI?
articles.summary: According to data from the US Census Bureau, the still-ongoing 2026 Transpacific container shipping peak season is not being driven by the boom in investments in artificial intelligence (AI) and is instead being actively fuelled by traditional consumer goods. articles.body: According to data from the US Census Bureau, the still-ongoing 2026 Transpacific container shipping peak season is not being driven by the boom in investments in artificial intelligence (AI) and is instead being actively fuelled by traditional consumer goods. Figure 1 shows the monthly Asia to US containerized imports in Metric Tons for January 2022 to September 2026, broken down into seven major categories. We mapped all HS8 codes in the data to five traditional container goods classification groups (A‑E) and created two new groups (F‑G). We do not claim that all goods transported under the F-G classifications are being used to build AI data centres, but that they could conceivably be contributing to it. Source: Sea-Intelligence.com, Sunday Spotlight, issue 790 The data shows that high‑value AI computer chips and IT equipment does not travel by ocean freight and is almost exclusively shipped by airfreight. Furthermore, when looking at the physical materials needed to build these massive data centres, the numbers show no significant impact on Asia-US volumes. The data shows that the import weight for data centre construction materials and infrastructure has remained almost completely flat. If the AI boom were truly driving Transpacific container volumes, we would expect to see an increase here. So, what is driving Transpacific volumes then? The 2026 peak season boom is being driven almost entirely by traditional container goods and raw manufacturing materials. We are seeing strong growth in the import of everyday consumer items like apparel, toys, games, sporting goods, and bicycles. Additionally, there are major increases in raw materials and intermediate goods like plastics, paper, packaging, and everyday hardware.

articles.title: Liquefied biogas storage tank installed at the port of Gothenburg
articles.summary: Construction of the biogas liquefaction plant at the Port of Gothenburg has reached an important milestone with the installation of the facility’s liquefied biogas storage tank. The plant is scheduled for completion in the second quarter of 2027 and is expected to make Swedish biogas more accessible to more sectors,...
articles.body: Construction of the biogas liquefaction plant at the Port of Gothenburg has reached an important milestone with the installation of the facility’s liquefied biogas storage tank. The plant is scheduled for completion in the second quarter of 2027 and is expected to make Swedish biogas more accessible to more sectors, not least shipping. LBG is a renewable, low-climate-impact fuel that can replace fossil alternatives, and interest in it is growing rapidly in the shipping sector. Groundworks, including foundations and base slabs, are complete, and the tank is the first of the plant’s key components to be installed. It arrived at the port by vessel, has a volume of 500 cubic metres, weighs close to 140 tonnes and will be able to store up to 200 tonnes of LBG once the facility is operational. Once finished, the plant will be able to deliver 250 gigawatt-hours of LBG a year, equivalent to the consumption of 500 trucks or the bunkering of 50 vessels. It will be the first liquefaction plant in Sweden connected directly to the west Swedish gas grid, creating a new market for Swedish biogas producers that are, or want to become, connected to the grid. Producers and users are already present at the port: ST1 Biokraft has signed an agreement securing part of the plant’s capacity, and several shipping companies that call regularly already use LBG to power their vessels. Therese Jällbrink, Head of Renewable Energy at the Port of Gothenburg, said shipping’s transition requires a collaborative value chain, that the facility strengthens the port’s position in renewable bunker fuels and allows LBG to be offered to shipping on a larger scale, and that the growing number of vessels on order for LBG operation points to strong potential for increased bunkering. Carolina Wistén, Head of Customer and Market, Gas Grid, at Nordion Energi, said the facility is starting to take shape and brings the goal of delivering LBG from the gas grid to shipping, heavy transport and industry closer.

articles.body: Hapag-Lloyd has announced an increase in its Freight All Kinds (FAK) ocean tariff rates for shipments from the Far East to Europe, effective from 1 December 2026, with the highest published rate reaching US$6,800 per 40-foot container. The revised tariffs will apply to 20-foot and 40-foot dry containers, including high-cube equipment, on sailings with a tariffing date on or after 1 December. The rates will remain in effect until further notice. Under the new tariff structure, shipments from the Far East to Northern Europe will be charged US$3,000 per 20-foot container and US$4,500 per 40-foot dry or high-cube container. For the Western Mediterranean and Adriatic, rates will reach US$5,100 per 20-foot container and US$6,400 per 40-foot container. Higher tariffs will apply to Türkiye, Egypt and the Eastern Mediterranean, at US$5,300 per 20-foot container and US$6,600 per 40-foot container. The highest rates will cover Black Sea destinations in Bulgaria and Romania, reaching US$5,450 and US$6,800, respectively. articles.title: GXO and Apptronik target deployment of up to 1,000 humanoid robots
articles.summary: GXO Logistics has signed a letter of intent with robotics developer Apptronik to expand the use of humanoid robots in warehouse operations. The companies are exploring a potential global deployment of up to 1,000 Apollo robots over the next four years. The agreement builds on their existing partnership and will...
articles.body: GXO Logistics has signed a letter of intent with robotics developer Apptronik to expand the use of humanoid robots in warehouse operations. The companies are exploring a potential global deployment of up to 1,000 Apollo robots over the next four years. The agreement builds on their existing partnership and will introduce further operational trials beginning in 2027. These trials will assess how humanoid robots can support warehouse activities and work alongside employees and existing automation systems. Under the proposed plan, the first commercial deployment could take place in North America in late 2027. However, any wider rollout will depend on the successful completion of trials and the achievement of agreed performance and safety targets. The companies also plan to develop a Robotics-as-a-Service (RaaS) commercial framework. This model would allow GXO to introduce humanoid robots through a service-based arrangement rather than relying entirely on conventional equipment purchases. Warehouse trials to assess operational performance The expanded trials will cover several warehouse activities, including order picking, packing, sortation and the movement of cases and totes. In addition, the companies will evaluate technical requirements, operational security and workplace safety. Each application will be assessed against agreed productivity and performance indicators before being considered for wider deployment. “Humanoid robots are the latest evolution of intelligent automation, and their increasing dexterity will make them one of the most transformative applications of physical AI in logistics,” said Patrick Kelleher, CEO, GXO. The partnership began in 2024 with a proof-of-concept programme focused on the use of Apollo robots in warehouse environments. Earlier in 2026, the companies completed a pilot deployment in the United States. The project focused on autonomous picking of small consumer goods in a live warehouse setting. GXO and Apptronik have also evaluated more than 50 different logistics tasks at Apptronik’s Robot Park training facility. These assessments included data collection and autonomous testing to examine potential applications. Potential expansion of humanoid automation The Apollo robot is designed to perform repetitive and physically demanding warehouse tasks. According to the companies, the technology could help improve operational productivity and address labour availability challenges. However, the planned deployment of up to 1,000 robots remains conditional. The companies must first demonstrate that the technology can meet operational, safety and performance requirements. The proposed rollout represents a further step in GXO’s efforts to integrate robotics and artificial intelligence into its logistics operations. GXO operates more than 1,000 facilities worldwide and employs over 150,000 people. Its activities include contract logistics, warehouse management and supply chain services for customers across multiple industries. The expanded collaboration will help determine whether humanoid robots can move beyond pilot projects and become a practical part of large-scale warehouse operations.

The extension comes just two days before a previous waiver was set to expire. It will take effect at 12 a.m. Monday New York time, ensuring no gap between the expiration of the prior one, the official said. The decision underscores the administration’s continued concerns about high energy costs due to the war in Iran , after Democrats trounced Republicans in the November midterm elections that were dominated by voter concerns about the cost of living. Trump did not change the breadth of the relief, after previously narrowing the waiver’s scope in August to require the government conduct case-by-case reviews of vessel availability. Read more: Maritime Industry Urges Trump to Let Jones Act Waiver Expire November 15 Shipbuilders and their allies on Capitol Hill had argued against any extension , saying they have undercut longstanding protectionist mandates they see as critical to bolstering domestic shipbuilding capacity. But oil and chemical companies said the waiver has helped move cargoes of crude, fertilizer and other commodities between US ports efficiently and at lower cost, helping counteract supply disruptions stoked by the war in Iran and refinery damage in Russia. Some 338 voyages have taken place on foreign vessels since Trump first waived Jones Act restrictions in March , including shipments of Texas crude to Pennsylvania and propane to Puerto Rico, according to government data analyzed by the Cato Institute. California has received the majority of shipments, with 23 million barrels of additional products carried to the state compared with 8 million barrels during the same period last year, the White House official said. An additional 90 million barrels of products — mostly refined fuels — have been shipped between US ports since the waiver was first issued, with gasoline, crude oil and renewable fuel being the biggest beneficiaries, according to the official. The current waiver has helped enable the transport of some 13 million barrels of products, more than a third of which has been gasoline, with about 28% crude oil. The waiver’s use, however, has shrunk after Trump limited its scope. Under the new approach, the US Maritime Administration needs to be consulted on the availability of US-flagged, -owned and -operated vessels before the waiver is applied to individual voyages. Products that benefit under the waiver include gasoline, jet fuel, crude oil, naphtha, liquefied natural gas, soy oil and fertilizers. Trump’s Jones Act exemption has been the longest and broadest waiver of the law in more than seven decades. Previous presidents have discretely lifted Jones Act mandates for individual voyages and short periods in the wake of hurricanes and pipeline outages that disrupted fuel flows. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. REUTERS/Christiana Botic TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY All passengers and crew aboard an American Cruise Lines riverboat survived after a Marshall Islands-flagged asphalt tanker struck the docked paddle-wheeler on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday, causing it to capsize and sending people into the water. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno confirmed that everyone aboard the American Heritage had been accounted for following a massive rescue operation. Thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals, including 30 passengers and two police officers, but none suffered critical injuries. “We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” Moreno said at a news conference. The 160-meter tanker Atlantic Asphalt struck the U.S.-flagged American Heritage at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time as it was traveling upbound on the Lower Mississippi River, just below the Crescent City Connection bridge, according to the Port of New Orleans. Video of the collision shows the much larger tanker striking the docked paddlewheeler, which began taking on water and listing heavily before eventually capsizing alongside the dock. Other footage shows people in the river wearing life jackets as tugboat operators, nearby vessel crews, police and emergency responders rushed to pull them to safety. The American Heritage had docked outside the Port of New Orleans Administration Building approximately two hours earlier to begin disembarking passengers following an eight-day Mississippi River cruise. Port officials initially reported approximately 129 passengers aboard, in addition to crew members. Moreno said passengers began evacuating after the initial impact, but the vessel overturned before everyone could get off, forcing rescuers to pull people from the water. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry praised the response, calling the outcome “nothing short of a miracle.” “While we will continue to work through the details of this incident, one thing is clear: our first responders on the national, state, and local level saved countless lives today, and for that I and all of our country are thankful!” Landry said. In an updated statement Friday, American Cruise Lines said it was arranging hotel accommodations and assistance for everyone who had been aboard the American Heritage . “We are getting everyone who was aboard the ship settled into hotels and making sure they have everything they need,” the company said. American Cruise Lines also thanked the U.S. Coast Guard, its crew and local first responders for their rescue efforts, adding that it remained in close contact with the Coast Guard, New Orleans Police and other agencies. The cause of the collision remains under investigation, although the U.S. Coast Guard said the tanker may have experienced a steering failure. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said the tanker appeared to have experienced “some type of loss of steering,” but emphasized that the exact cause had not been determined. The National Transportation Safety Board has launched an investigation and is sending a team to New Orleans, with investigators expected to arrive Saturday morning. The Coast Guard also closed the Mississippi River to vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96 while emergency operations continued, temporarily disrupting navigation along one of the nation’s busiest commercial waterways. Officials said they were evaluating when the waterway could safely reopen. According to MarineTraffic , the Atlantic Asphalt is a 160-meter asphalt and bitumen tanker sailing under the Marshall Islands flag. The American Heritage is an 81-meter U.S.-flagged paddlewheel cruise ship built in 2015 with accommodations for up to 150 passengers. AIS data shows the Atlantic Asphalt called at Amuay, Venezuela, in October before arriving in Paulsboro, New Jersey. The tanker departed Paulsboro on October 26 and arrived in New Orleans on November 11, two days before the collision. The investigation will focus on what caused the tanker to strike the docked passenger vessel along the busy Lower Mississippi River, where deep-draft oceangoing ships regularly navigate in close proximity to river cruise vessels, tugs and barges. articles.summary: Global oil markets are beginning to recover from the Iran war, but shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted, with vessel traffic roughly 65% below pre-conflict levels and...
