Join the leading maritime news network FILE PHOTO: Oil/Chemical Tanker "Bald Man" at the Port of Fujairah, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran limits marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, in Fujairah, United Arab Emirates, May 6, 2026. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo Global oil markets are beginning to recover from the Iran war, but shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted, with vessel traffic roughly 65% below pre-conflict levels and tanker attacks continuing across the region. Separate reports released Friday by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) highlight the uneven recovery in energy trade nearly nine months after the conflict began. The IEA said global oil supplies are on track to exceed demand by 1.7 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, reversing its previous forecast of a deficit as Persian Gulf producers restore disrupted exports. Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, climbed to 18.4 million barrels per day in October, just 26% below pre-war levels. Crude shipments accounted for much of the recovery, reaching 15 million barrels per day, or about 82% of pre-war volumes. Yet the rebound in oil shipments has not translated into a broader recovery in vessel traffic. Hormuz Traffic Remains Deeply Disrupted In its latest weekly assessment, UKMTO reported 139 outbound and 169 inbound transits through the Strait of Hormuz, with overall traffic still approximately 65% below pre-conflict levels. The figures combine AIS-tracked vessel movements with U.S.-reported facilitated transits, including ships operating without broadcasting AIS signals. UKMTO cautioned that it could not independently verify the U.S. figures. The security situation remains dangerous. UKMTO documented eight maritime security incidents during its latest reporting period, including seven tanker attacks. Five incidents occurred in the Strait of Hormuz, two in the Arabian Gulf and one in the Gulf of Oman. Three vessels continued their voyages, three required assistance and the outcomes of two remained unknown. None was reported sunk. UKMTO also noted that while most AIS-broadcasting vessels continue to use the Iranian route, more ships are using the southern passage. Most reported projectile strikes since July 6 have occurred along that southern route. More Oil Moving, But Shipping Costs Remain High The recovery in Gulf exports is beginning to ease pressure on global oil markets. According to the IEA, observed oil inventories increased by 52 million barrels in October, while oil volumes on the water jumped by 86 million barrels to their highest level since January. For tanker operators, however, conditions remain difficult. Freight rates for crude shipments from the Middle East to Asia remain near record levels, according to the IEA, even as rates for Aframax and Suezmax tankers have eased. The contrast underscores the uneven recovery. While Gulf producers have restored substantial crude export volumes, commercial shipping continues to operate under significant security constraints. The IEA’s October export figures and UKMTO’s November vessel counts measure different periods and activity, but together point to a market recovering faster than normal shipping conditions. The improvement has also been concentrated in crude oil. Gulf exports of refined products and liquefied petroleum gas remain at roughly half their pre-war levels, contributing to persistent shortages. Diesel is particularly tight, with European prices still near $180 per barrel, roughly 77% above pre-war levels. To ease the shortage, IEA member countries plan to make another 71 million barrels of emergency stocks available by the end of February, including 15 million barrels of diesel. Meanwhile, the recovery in oil supplies has helped push crude prices sharply lower. articles.body: CMA CGM Demonstrates Relative Resilience in a Volatile Q3 Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 13, 2026 © Michael Derrer Fuchs - stock.adobe.com The third quarter of 2026 took place in a volatile economic environment, with persistent tensions in the Middle East impacting international trade and global supply chains. In this context, both shipping and logistics activities were affected by adjustments made to trade routes and transport networks. Nevertheless, the global economy demonstrated relative resilience given the scale of the shock to energy prices, while international trade remained dynamic. The Group’s transported volumes increased by 5.5% compared with the third quarter of 2025, outperforming the market. This represents one of the strongest growth rates recorded in recent years. This growth was underpinned by three key drivers: Restocking , as companies sought to build up inventories amid ongoing economic and geopolitical uncertainty; Increased investment in AI-related infrastructure and data centres; Strong momentum in clean technologies and electric vehicles , particularly in China, amid higher hydrocarbon prices. The CMA CGM Group leveraged the complementary strengths of its shipping, logistics and terminal operations to offer customers integrated solutions across the entire supply chain. This strategy is underpinned by investments in port infrastructure, which are essential to expanding the Group’s capacity and strengthening its global network. The Group also accelerated its transformation through innovation and artificial intelligence across all its businesses. MAIA, its agentic AI platform co-developed with Mistral AI, is being progressively rolled out to employees across its shipping, logistics and media businesses. In France, the CMA CGM Group confirms its long-term commitment and contribution to the country's economic, maritime and logistics development. The Group supports 96,500 jobs, including 19,100 direct jobs and 77,400 jobs across the wider economy. The Group has welcomed the first vessels in its new series of 24,000-TEU containerships, including the CMA CGM NOTRE DAME, CMA CGM PANTHEON and CMA CGM ORSAY, which are deployed on its flagship FAL service connecting Asia and Europe. These are the world's largest LNG-powered containerships operating under the French flag. CMA CGM also accelerated the energy transition in shipping through several major alternative fuel bunkering operations: bioethanol in Brazil, bio-LNG in Rotterdam and a world-record biomethanol bunkering operation in Shanghai. CEVA Logistics expanded its international footprint through the acquisition of FedEx Supply Chain and initiated a simplification of its organizational structure under the leadership of Patrick Moebel, aimed at improving its efficiency and strengthening customer proximity CMA CGM further developed its global terminal network, notably through Terminal 4 at the Port of Jeddah in partnership with Red Sea Gateway Terminal, and CMA Terminals' acquisition of a 49% stake in Nador Container Terminal in Morocco. CMA CGM AIR CARGO strengthened its operations during the quarter, with a fleet of eight aircraft now operating under the CMA CGM AIR CARGO and Air Belgium brands, supported by hubs in France, Belgium and the United States. CMA Media launched CMA Sport, while BFMTV maintained its position as France's leading news channel throughout the quarter. Outlook Demand for maritime transport benefited from a strong increase in volumes carried, a trend that is expected to continue over the coming months. Freight rates, which have been rising since the second quarter of 2026, are also supporting the growth of the business. However, the outlook for the coming months remains uncertain. Tensions in the Middle East continue to disrupt shipping routes and weigh on operating costs, while changes in trade policies will continue to influence international trade flows. Against this backdrop, the CMA CGM Group maintains a prudent and responsive approach to management. Its presence across the entire logistics chain, the flexibility of its network and the strength of its balance sheet are major assets in order to cope with changes in its operating environment and provide long-term support to its customers.

articles.summary: The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping.

REUTERS/Mohammed Aty LONDON, Nov 13 – The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping. The agency also gave more details of remaining volumes to come from a record release of oil from its members’ emergency reserves pledged in March, saying 71 million barrels would be made available by the end of February including 15 million barrels of diesel to ease market tightness. Oil supply will average 105 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, the Paris-based agency, which advises industrialized countries, said in a monthly report, 1.7 million bpd higher than forecast demand. The IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit. “The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran,” the agency said in the report. Oil prices reversed earlier gains after the IEA report was released at 0900 GMT. Brent crude LCOc1 was last down 0.1% at $95.71 a barrel. The report follows signs that Gulf oil producers are recovering exports disrupted since the start of the war in late February by using workarounds such as so-called dark crossings through the Strait of Hormuz, where tankers switch off tracking signals to evade attack. The OPEC+ group, which includes the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia, pumped 41.23 million bpd of crude in October, OPEC said on Wednesday, up about 2.04 million bpd from September and 97% of the pre-war February volume. OTHER ANALYSTS SEE SIGNS OF SURPLUS Other analysts have also forecast a return to excess supply, despite the lack of a resolution to the Iran war and continuing tanker attacks in the Gulf. JPMorgan last week forecast a global surplus of 1.4 million bpd in October. High oil prices have also curbed demand this year, helping tip the balance into a surplus. World oil demand is forecast to fall by 2.7 million bpd in 2026 to 102.3 million bpd before rebounding by 2 million bpd in 2027, the IEA said, little changed from its previous forecasts. As well as rising output from OPEC+, the IEA flagged supply rising from outside the group. Production from the United States, Canada, Brazil, Argentina and Guyana will rise by 1.6 million bpd this year, the IEA said. In 2027, global supply is projected to rise by 6.6 million bpd to 108.1 million bpd, led by a further recovery in Gulf output. Still, the 2027 supply growth forecast is down 1.1 million bpd from last month’s report, and the lower outlook partly reflects a downward revision from Iran, the IEA said. Iran is subject to a US blockade that has curbed its oil exports. For 2027, the IEA sees the supply surplus at about 3.8 million bpd, slightly down from a 3.94 million bpd surplus last month. Singapore also maintained its leading position in three of the five pillars* assessed in the report — Shipping, Ports and Logistics, and Attractiveness and Competitiveness. The LMC report benchmarks leading maritime cities based on objective indicators, including shipping activity, port performance and maritime business services, as well as assessments by maritime industry experts worldwide. Home to over 200 international shipping groups and a wide range of maritime service providers, Singapore’s continued recognition as a leading maritime city reflects the strength of its maritime ecosystem, which brings together global connectivity, port and logistics capabilities, maritime services, talent and innovation. These complementary strengths provide maritime companies with access to markets, business opportunities and specialized expertise, making Singapore an attractive location for companies to establish their presence and grow their businesses. This ecosystem is supported by Singapore’s position as one of the world’s busiest ports, connected to more than 600 ports worldwide. In 2025, the Port of Singapore handled a record 44.66 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in container throughput and 3.22 billion gross tonnage in vessel arrival. Singapore also remained the world’s largest bunkering port, with marine fuel sales reaching a record 56.77 million tonnes. Continued investments in port automation, maritime digitalization, innovation and the adoption of alternative marine fuels further strengthen the ecosystem and create new opportunities for maritime businesses. articles.body: Singapore-Registered Bulk Carrier Strikes US Bridge, Disrupts Traffic Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 13, 2026 The Tacony-Palmyra Bridge spanning the Delaware River between Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and Palmyra, New Jersey, pictured in June 2010 (Credit: Jag9889 / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0) The Singapore-registered bulk carrier STRATEGIC ALLIANCE has struck the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge over the Delaware River between Pennsylvania and New Jersey, forcing a temporary closure before vehicle traffic was partially restored. The incident occurred shortly after 1 p.m. local time on November 12 during a bridge opening for marine traffic, according to the Burlington County Bridge Commission. Representative Ed Neilson reported that the bridge was initially unable to close following the collision, causing significant traffic congestion on the Philadelphia side. The bridge was closed to motorists and pedestrians while officials investigated potential structural damage. Subsequent inspections indicated that the bridge was safe and that the damage appeared minor, the commission said. By 8:40 p.m., two lanes had reopened to motor vehicles, one in each direction, although another lane remained closed for repairs to the pedestrian sidewalk. Pedestrian access to the bridge remained prohibited. Singapore's Maritime and Port Authority (MPA) confirmed that STRATEGIC ALLIANCE was involved in the incident, reporting no injuries to civilians or crew members, no major damage to the vessel and no marine pollution. The bulk carrier is safely moored at the Kinder Morgan terminal in Pennsylvania, according to MPA. The Singaporean authority said it was in contact with the vessel's management company and relevant US authorities to establish the circumstances of the incident and would conduct an investigation. Repairs and inspections of the bridge are continuing.

November 13, 2026 (Credit: Seaway7) Seaway7 has installed the first inter-array cable at Ørsted's 2.9 GW Hornsea 3 offshore wind farm in the UK North Sea, marking the start of a major cable installation campaign. The Hornsea projects are located approximately 90 - 160 kilometers off the east coast of England, in water depths ranging from around 25 to 75 meters. articles.body: Containers Contributions From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping Splash November 13, 2026 0 14,703 3 minutes read Dr Raymon Krishnan, president of Singapore’s Logistics & Supply Chain Management Society, writes for Splash today, reflecting on one of this week’s most talked about stories in the mainstream press. On Wednesday, the 990-foot ocean liner SS United States was deliberately sunk off Destin, Florida , to become what is expected to be the world’s largest artificial reef. Initial underwater inspections found the vessel upright, approximately 180 feet below the surface. The sinking of the SS United States reminds us that ships can outlive their commercial purpose. Launched in 1951 and entering service in 1952, the SS United States was the pinnacle of post-war American maritime engineering. It held the record as the world’s fastest passenger ship but was withdrawn in 1969 as commercial aviation transformed the economics of transatlantic travel. It was not poor engineering that made the ship obsolete, it was a market that had moved on. After decades moored in Philadelphia, the vessel was acquired by Okaloosa County in a project valued at approximately $13m. Its new role will support tourism, marine conservation and research. Its retirement offers a useful perspective on container shipping as it now faces another turning point. A substantial wave of new capacity The container shipping industry is preparing for a significant increase in fleet capacity. According to Drewry’s third-quarter 2026 Container Forecaster the global containership orderbook stood at approximately 13.9m teu on 1 September 2026, equivalent to 40.9% of the active fleet. Drewry forecasts fleet growth of 8.4% in 2027, rising to 12.1% in 2028 before moderating to 9.4% in 2029. The concern is the market into which these ships will be delivered. During the pandemic, congestion, equipment shortages and route disruption absorbed vessel capacity. Diversions around the Cape of Good Hope lengthened voyages and tied up ships. Carriers responded by ordering larger, more fuel-efficient vessels anticipating continued trade growth, but shipbuilding schedules are long and in the era of the never normal, market conditions change quickly. If Red Sea and Suez Canal routings return progressively to normal, shorter voyages could release significant effective capacity without a single additional ship entering service. Combined with newbuildings, this could widen the gap between supply and demand. Vessel capacity could potentially reach as much as 10% above demand under such circumstances. The consequences could include lower freight rates, tougher competition for cargo, blank sailings, slower steaming, vessel idling and accelerated recycling of older tonnage. The industry faces a major capacity-management challenge. The cost of getting the timing wrong Aviation permanently changed the market for passenger liners, while container shipping remains essential to trade. New vessels will not automatically become redundant. Nevertheless, ships are long-term capital investments, ordered years before delivery and expected to earn returns over operating lives spanning decades. A vessel ordered when freight rates are high and capacity constrained may enter service when demand is weaker, transit times are shorter and competing tonnage is plentiful. Efficiency alone cannot guarantee a satisfactory return. Carriers will have to decide which vessels to deploy, which trades to prioritise and when to redeploy or retire older ships. Smaller vessels displaced from mainline routes may move into regional trades, adding competitive pressure whilst others may be laid up, sold or recycled. Ports and terminals may see service patterns, berth requirements and transhipment flows change. Shippers may welcome lower rates but carriers protecting utilisation may consolidate services, withdraw sailings or alter port rotations. Lower prices could therefore come with less predictable frequency and transit times. The costs of poor capacity planning will ultimately ripple through businesses to end users and consumers. A different future for ageing vessels The SS United States project raises the question of what happens when ships lose their original commercial purpose. Conversion into an artificial reef offers a potential tourism and conservation role but it is neither a universal nor necessarily economical solution for commercial vessels. For surplus container ships, recycling will remain the principal end-of-life option when redeployment is no longer viable. Some older vessels may serve feeder networks or specialised trades, provided their economics remain competitive. Fleet renewal should consider the economic, environmental and operational consequences of retiring existing tonnage and not just the efficiency gains promised by newbuildings. The SS United States was a remarkable engineering achievement but it could not escape changing transportation economics. Its story reminds us that a ship’s commercial lifespan is determined not simply by how well it is built but by whether the market still needs what it does. As the industry approaches 2027, the question is whether carriers have ordered more capacity than the market can sustainably absorb and how prepared they are to manage the consequences. The challenge is not simply to build the next generation of vessels. It is to ensure there is a commercially sustainable reason to put them to work. It’s not something we as an industry have a good track doing. articles.body: Asia Gas BW LPG scores another lucrative Avance VLGC flip Adis Ajdin November 13, 2026 0 1,115 1 minute read Geir Vinnes / Marine Traffic Geir Vinnes / Marine Traffic BW LPG has struck another lucrative vessel sale, offloading a VLGC acquired in John Fredriksen’s Avance Gas fleet deal less than two years ago for well over $100m. The New York- and Oslo-listed gas carrier giant has agreed to sell the 2015-built, 83,134 cu m BW Mistral , with the transaction expected to generate a net book gain of around $37m and net cash proceeds of approximately $104m. The buyer has not been disclosed. Built at China’s Jiangnan shipyard, the scrubber-fitted vessel is currently trading in the spot market and will continue earning revenue for BW LPG until its scheduled handover by mid-January 2027. Chief executive Kristian Sørensen said the ship had contributed significantly to earnings since joining the fleet in 2024, with the company now taking advantage of strong secondhand values to realise a sizeable return. The disposal marks another profitable exit from the 12-ship Avance Gas fleet acquired in August 2024 for $1.05bn in cash, shares and assumed debt. In July, BW LPG agreed to sell the 2015-built, 83,000 cu m BW Levant , another vessel from the Avance transaction, with expected net cash proceeds of $38m and a book gain of around $17m. The two deals are set to generate combined book gains of approximately $54m and net cash proceeds of $142m. The latest sale comes amid a broader fleet renewal drive at BW LPG. Its 52%-owned Indian subsidiary has also been selling older VLGCs, most recently agreeing to dispose of the 2008-built BW Loyalty for a price in the low-$80m range, with an expected gain of $52m. At the other end of the fleet, BW LPG has committed around $940m to eight 90,000 cu m panamax VLGC newbuildings at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea, scheduled for delivery between 2029 and 2030. articles.body: Oil Heads for Weekly Decline Despite Middle East Supply Threats Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 13, 2026 © Miha Creative / Adobe Stock Oil prices edged up on Friday but were headed for a second weekly decline as the continued US focus on its blockade and economic pressure on Iran eased fears of renewed fighting in the Middle East, though shipping attacks remained a supply risk. Brent futures LCOc1 were up 53 cents, or 0.55%, to $96.35 a barrel at 0900 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures CLc1 added 20 cents, or 0.23%, to $88.94 a barrel. For the week, Brent and WTI were both on track for a 2% drop. The benchmarks plunged 16% and 13%, respectively, last week. "The market is range bound post midterms. The ability for more hostilities (in Iran) is restricted but a deal is equally elusive," said Jeff Currie, founder of Real Macro and former global head of commodities research at Goldman Sachs. "That means the market is roughly balanced, with the ability to trade up limited and the ability to trade down limited," he said. Oil has had a volatile trading week, with earlier hopes for a rapprochement in the US-Israeli war on Iran, now in its ninth month, offset by strikes on Saudi Arabian infrastructure by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and attacks on tankers shipping crude out of the Gulf. US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social a deal with Iran was not necessary to end the war. "Trump's indications that further military escalation against Iran may not be necessary have raised expectations that Washington could increasingly rely on economic sanctions and restrictions on oil shipments rather than intensifying military operations," said Sugandha Sachdeva, founder of SS WealthStreet, a New Delhi-based research firm. The weakness in oil prices is also largely driven by signs of softening US demand, as rising crude oil and fuel inventories indicate a relatively subdued consumption outlook, Sachdeva said. US crude and fuel inventories rose last week, driven by softer refined products demand and a jump in oil imports, the Energy Information Administration said on Thursday. Despite the easing prices, risks remain for oil shipments out of the Strait of Hormuz, the key waterway for crude exports from the main Middle East producers. On Thursday, Iran's military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings. Reuters could not immediately verify the Iranian accounts. That same day, Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they had attacked a pumping station on the Saudi East-West oil pipeline, an oil facility in the Saudi Red Sea city of Yanbu, and an Aramco building in the capital Riyadh. "Geopolitical risks remain elevated, and any fresh disruption to oil supplies could quickly reignite upward pressure on prices," Sachdeva of SS WealthStreet said. articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Finance and Insurance Greater China Cetus seals $200m share placement ahead of Oslo debut Adis Ajdin November 13, 2026 0 744 1 minute read Cetus Maritime Cetus Maritime Hong Kong-based dry bulk owner Cetus Maritime has successfully placed a NOK1.89bn ($200m) share offering, including an over-allotment, clearing a major hurdle ahead of its planned Oslo stock market debut next week. The Mark Young-led company said it had conditionally allocated 108.5m shares at NOK17.44 ($1.83) apiece, taking up the full $25m over-allotment on top of its original $175m fundraising target. The transaction comprises 95m new shares raising approximately $174m for Cetus, alongside 13.5m existing shares borrowed from major shareholder Pacific Transportation Asia (PTA) to cover the over-allotment. A 30-day greenshoe option could bring in further capital through the issuance of additional new shares. The placement follows strong initial interest from some of shipping’s biggest investment names, including an affiliate of Idan Ofer’s Eastern Pacific Shipping, Arne Blystad’s Songa Capital and the Albemarle Shipping Fund, co-founded by Magnus Halvorsen. Together with DNB Asset Management, the four investors had indicated interest in subscribing for a combined $106.5m. Cetus has not disclosed their final individual allocations. The proceeds should help fund Cetus’s acquisition of 13 handysize and ultramax bulkers from Hong Kong-listed Seacon Shipping Group, along with Syngrace, which holds contracts for three additional handysize newbuildings. The transaction involves approximately $72.5m in cash and the issuance of 37.3m Cetus shares to Seacon. The fresh capital will also support newbuilding payments, fleet deleveraging and working capital requirements. Following completion of the fleet acquisition and a planned vessel sale, Cetus said it expects to operate 42 ships, comprising 34 vessels on the water and eight newbuildings scheduled for delivery in 2027 and 2028. The company is targeting November 18 for its first day of trading on Euronext Growth Oslo, subject to regulatory approvals and completion of the Seacon transaction. Cetus has also left the door open for a move to the main Oslo Børs list within 12 months of its debut. Following the listing and assuming full exercise of the greenshoe option, PTA would retain approximately 40.6% of the company, while Seacon would hold around 14.3%. articles.body: Europe Gas Operations Regulatory Tankers UK blacklists 11 ships in fresh Russia sanctions sweep Adis Ajdin November 13, 2026 1 1,296 1 minute read Afrelino Christian Mantiri / Marine Traffic Afrelino Christian Mantiri / Marine Traffic Britain has slapped fresh sanctions on 11 ships linked to Russian energy exports, targeting five LNG carriers, five oil tankers and a floating storage unit in its latest effort to disrupt Moscow’s seaborne oil and gas trade. The measures also cover nine companies, including Russian oil producer Slavneft, Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project and several energy trading businesses based in Dubai. The latest vessel additions include LNG carriers Melicertes, Neleus, Perle, Aeolus and Oneiroi , alongside the Novatek-linked Koryak FSU . On the oil side, London has blacklisted Apeks, Sara Sky, Balu 6, Yvika and Alma . The vessels operate under a mix of Russian, Panamanian, Sierra Leonean and Djiboutian flags, according to the official sanctions notice. The restrictions prohibit the specified ships from accessing British ports and impose controls on chartering and operating them. They also restrict the provision of services including ship finance, broking, technical assistance and crewing, subject to applicable exceptions and licensing arrangements. The corporate additions extend the crackdown beyond individual ships. Dubai-based Forteza Trading, Patera and Novus Energy have been designated, with British authorities specifically linking Novus Energy to dealings involving vessels already subject to UK restrictions. Russian petrochemical producer Sibur and coal groups SUEK and Kuzbassrazrezugol also feature in the latest package. The move brings all ten of Russia’s largest oil producers under British sanctions following the inclusion of Slavneft. The government announced the measures during the European Political Community summit in Dublin, where pressure on Russian energy revenues formed part of discussions on Ukraine. Britain has been steadily expanding its maritime restrictions this year, including sanctions against six ships in August and an earlier package targeting Russia’s developing LNG shadow fleet. articles.body: Project & Tenders November 13, 2026 · 1 minute ago Marine license granted for one of UK’s largest power projects NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email SSEN Transmission SSEN Transmission has secured the marine license for subsea cable infrastructure in Scottish waters for the 2 GW Eastern Green Link 3 (EGL3) high-voltage subsea electricity link between Scotland and England. EGL3, a joint venture between SSEN Transmission and National Grid Electricity Transmission (NGET), will run between Longside in Aberdeenshire and Walpole in Norfolk. Related Articles Cabling Marine license application filed for one of UK’s largest power projects 2 min read The marine license, awarded on November 11, covers the installation and operation of the project’s subsea cable infrastructure in Scottish waters, including nearshore work where the cable will meet land near Peterhead in Aberdeenshire. This follows several years of project development, marine surveys and ecological and environmental assessment work to understand the habitats and species present along the proposed cable route. “We’re absolutely delighted to have been granted the marine licence for the Scottish waters section of the subsea cable route on EGL3. This marks a really significant moment for the project and reflects many years of design development and marine survey activities which have underpinned this successful outcome today," said James Johnson , Joint Venture Program Director at SSEN Transmission. “Developing infrastructure of this scale in the marine environment requires careful planning and collaboration. Throughout the development, we have worked closely with local communities, marine stakeholders and other offshore developers and asset owners, whose feedback has helped shape our plans and minimise potential impacts wherever possible." Construction of EGL3 is proposed to start in 2029, with the aim of the link being fully operational by 2033. Under a contract worth over €2.2 billion , NKT will deliver a turnkey scope to design, manufacture, and install a 525 kV HVDC power cable system with a route length of around 680 kilometers, including onshore and offshore cable sections, for the project. Hitachi Energy will deliver HVDC converter stations in Scotland and England.
